paras: The lynching of Jesse Franklin and Jim Phillips was the fatal whipping of two Black men by a band of white men in the Bunker Hill community of Rusk County, Texas, in early October 1903. Both men died, and four white men were reported arrested. The case became national news when Webster Flanagan, the federal internal revenue collector for the district, said local news of the attacks had been suppressed and asked Governor Lanham for protection.

According to Flanagan, bands of white men had for several weeks carried out "murders and cruelties" against Black people in Rusk County, and an order had gone out that all must leave so that it would be "a white man's county." The Henderson Times, owned by R. T. Milner, a former Speaker of the Texas House, traced the trouble to the whipping of "a few trifling negroes" in Henderson who were warned to go to work, an example that grew into vengeance on "harmless and helpless" Black people across the county.

A few nights before Flanagan arrived, two Black men he called among "the most peaceable and inoffensive" were taken from their homes by a band of white men, stripped, tied to trees and whipped. Flanagan told the New York Sun that the lash was rawhide on an oak handle, with nails protruding nearly half an inch, and that the men were whipped into insensibility. No accusation against either man appears in the coverage.

One man died on Saturday night, October 10, and Flanagan said the other could not recover. The Henderson Times later named the two as Jesse Franklin and Jim Phillips of the Bunker Hill community and reported that both "were whipped, lingered, suffered and finally died."

On October 14 Flanagan, who said the attackers were "well known" and four were in jail at Henderson, asked Lanham to protect the Black residents, warning that he would otherwise appeal to federal authorities. The next day Lanham refused his request for state troops, declaring the situation "not as serious as reported," but on October 16 he instructed the county's district judge and peace authorities to leave nothing undone to punish the guilty.

County citizens reportedly passed resolutions calling for protection of Black residents, and by October 21 Lanham was making "a rigid investigation." The arrested men are not named, and no report of an inquest, indictment or trial was found.

Flanagan's statement ran on October 15 in the New-York Tribune and the Sun by their own telegrams, and in a Record-Herald special and a wire version reprinted from Washington to Salt Lake City. Headlines stressed torture and death: "Negroe Tortured to Death" in the Tribune and "Negroes Wantonly Outraged in Texas" in the Deseret Evening News. Southern papers carried the wire text as well, the Savannah Morning News under "Inoffensive Blacks Beaten to Death" and the Keowee Courier under "Blacks Lashed Until They Die," while the Richmond Times Dispatch chose "Alleges Cruelty to the Negroes."

The San Antonio Daily Light gave the story one line but remarked editorially that "Lanham thinks that the negroes in Rusk county need no protection, but not so the people." Milner's editorial, calling the killings "some of the most atrocious crimes ever committed by white men," was carried by the Sun on October 21 and reprinted by the Weekly Arizona Journal-Miner, which likened the atrocities to those reported from Turkey and Macedonia.

Black newspapers took up the story late in October, from the same sources. The Sedalia Weekly Conservator reprinted Milner's editorial under "Texas Editor Denounces Lawlessness Against Negroes," and the Professional World headed its brief "A White Man's County." The Topeka Plaindealer's editorial "Is It Coming?" set Flanagan's appeal beside a Tennessee coroner's verdict against lynchers as signs of changing Southern sentiment and commended both for their "nerve."

Early reports differed on the toll: Flanagan said one man had died and the other could not recover, while the Record-Herald version spoke of "torturing to death two inoffensive blacks." The local Henderson Times, writing about a week later, said both men died, consistent with Flanagan's prognosis. Lanham's remark that the situation was not as serious as reported did not address the deaths.

bases: Two Black men taken from their homes by a band of white men were whipped and both died (A2, A3, A18); the attack was part of a whitecap campaign to drive Black residents from Rusk County (A2, A7).

A band of white men, four of whom were arrested, took the two men from their homes and whipped them, and both died (A2, A3, A18); the only reason reported was that Rusk was to be made 'a white man's county' (A2, A3).
Flanagan's statement from his visit (A2, A3) is independently confirmed by the Henderson Times, the local paper at the county seat, which names both victims as dead (A18, A21, A23).

accounts.label: Flanagan's statement
accounts.gist: Two inoffensive Black men were taken from their homes by a band of white men, stripped, tied and whipped with a nail-studded lash; one died and the other could not recover; four men arrested; all Black people ordered to leave the county.

accounts.label: Henderson Times (R. T. Milner)
accounts.gist: A wave of lawlessness that began with whipping Black men in Henderson spread through the county; Jesse Franklin and Jim Phillips of Bunker Hill were whipped and both died.

accounts.label: Governor Lanham
accounts.gist: The situation was not as serious as reported, and troops were not needed; he later ordered county officers to punish the guilty.

accounts.label: Black editorial comment
accounts.gist: Flanagan's appeal was a welcome sign of changing sentiment in the South; the Henderson paper confirmed a plan to make Rusk a white man's county.

framing.detail: The Tribune and Sun ran their own telegrams under 'Negroe Tortured to Death' and 'Torture of Negroes', relaying Flanagan's description of the victims as peaceable and inoffensive.

Wire versions ran nationally and in the South, headlined 'Inoffensive Blacks Beaten to Death' (Savannah), 'Blacks Lashed Until They Die' (Keowee) and the more guarded 'Alleges Cruelty to the Negroes' (Richmond).
The Weekly Arizona Journal-Miner's 'Terrible Arraignment' likened the atrocities to Turkey and Macedonia and quoted the Henderson editor at length.
The San Antonio Daily Light gave the news a single line but chided Lanham for thinking the Black residents needed no protection.
The Sedalia Weekly Conservator reprinted the Henderson editorial as 'Texas Editor Denounces Lawlessness Against Negroes'; the Professional World headed its brief 'A White Man's County'.
The Topeka Plaindealer's 'Is It Coming?' commended Flanagan's 'nerve' and blamed 'Negro haters' for the South's stagnation.
